source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα φύρων τὸν λόγον καὶ τὰ ὑπὸ αἱρέσεώς τινος λεγόμενα ὡς κοινὰ Χριστιανῶν ἐγκλήματα πᾶσι τοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ θείου προσάγων λόγου φησὶν ὅτι θεοῦ οὐκ ἂν εἴη τοιοῦτον σῶμα, οἷον τὸ σόν. ἀλλ᾿ ἡμεῖς πρὸς ταῦτα σῶμα αὐτὸν λέγομεν ἀνειληφέναι ὡς ἀπὸ θηλείας τῷ βίῳ ἐπιδημήσαντα ἀνθρώπινον καὶ θανάτου ἀνθρωπίνου δεκτικόν. διὸ πρὸς τοῖς ἄλλοις αὐτόν φαμεν καὶ μέγαν ἀγωνιστὴν γεγονέναι, διὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον σῶμα „πεπειρασμένον“ μὲν ὁμοίως πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις „κατὰ πάντα“ οὐκέτι δ᾿ ὡς ἄνθρωποι μεθ᾿ ἁμαρτίας ἀλλὰ πάντῃ „χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας.“ τρανῶς γὰρ ἡμῖν φαίνεται „ὅτι ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἐποίησεν, οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτοῦ“· καὶ „μὴ γνόντα“ αὐτὸν „ἁμαρτίαν“ ὡς καθαρὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ πάντων τῶν ἡμαρτηκότων ὁ θεός. εἶτα ὁ Κέλσος φησὶν ὅτι οὐκ ἂν εἴη θεοῦ σῶμα τὸ οὕτω σπαρὲν, ὡς σὺ, ὦ Ἰησοῦ, ἐσπάρης. πλὴν ὑπείδετο ὅτι εἰ, ὡς γέγραπται, γεγέννητο, δύναταί πως εἶναι τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ καὶ θειότερον παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς καὶ κατά τι σημαινόμενον θεοῦ σῶμα. ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἀπιστεῖ τοῖς ἀναγραφεῖσι περὶ τῆς ἐξ ἁγίου πνεύματος συλλήψεως αὐτοῦ καὶ πιστεύει αὐτὸν ὑπό τινος Πανθήρα φθείραντος τὴν παρθένον ἐσπάρθαι· διόπερ εἶπεν ὅτι οὐκ ἂν εἴη θεοῦ σῶμα οὕτω σπαρὲν, ὡς σὺ ἐσπάρης. ἀλλὰ γὰρ περὶ τούτων ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω πλείονα εἰρήκαμεν.
pass_a_gloss: After these things, having brought forward the discourse and the things said by some heresy as common faults of Christians to all from the divine discourse, he says that God would not have such a body as yours. But we say that he took on a body as from a female, having come to human life, and capable of human death. Therefore, among other things, we say that he also became a great athlete, because the human body, having been tempted in the same way as all humans in all things, no longer as humans with sin, but in every way without sin. For it clearly appears to us that he did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; and God handed him over, not knowing sin, as pure on behalf of all those who had sinned. Then Celsus says that the body would not be God's, having been sown in such a way, as you, Jesus, were sown. But he pretended that if, as it is written, he had been born, it might be possible for his body to be more divine than that of many and to be called God's body in some sense. But because he disbelieves the things written about his conception from the Holy Spirit and believes that he was sown by some Panther who corrupted the virgin, he said that the body would not be God's, having been sown in such a way, as you were sown. But we have said more about these things above.

choices.why: metaphorical sense of one who struggles or competes
passive sense of being tested or tried
mythological figure used to mock the virgin birth

bible_refs.note: he did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth

pass_b_english: After this, Celsus brings forward the discourse and the charges that some heresy levels as common faults of Christians, addressing them to everyone who draws near to the divine discourse, and he declares that God would never have a body like yours. We, on the other hand, confess that he took on a body by coming from a woman to dwell in human life, making it capable of human death. That is why, among other things, we also call him a great athlete: his human body was tested in the same way as every other human being in all respects, yet not as humans with sin, but in every way without sin. For it is perfectly clear to us that he committed no sin, nor was any deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22); and God handed him over, though he knew no sin, as a pure offering on behalf of all who had sinned. Then Celsus asserts that a body sown in such a way could not be God's body, just as you, Jesus, were sown. He concedes, however, that if, as it is written, he had been born, his body might somehow be more divine than most and be called God's body in some sense. But because he disbelieves the accounts written about his conception by the Holy Spirit and instead believes that he was sown by a certain Panther who corrupted the virgin, he concludes that such a body could not be God's. We have already said more about these matters above.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Greek text. Pass A and Pass B both preserve the nuances of the Greek, including the distinction between the human body being 'tested' (πεπειρασμένον) and the theological claim of sinlessness. Pass B correctly identifies the implicit scripture reference in 'μη γνόντα αὐτὸν ἁμαρτίαν' as 1 Peter 2:22. The title 'Christ's Body' correctly names the thought of the passage.
